---
title: "Lab 03: Resampling Methods"
---

This lab uses resampling to compare predictive models. The first half
uses the `Carseats` data to compare two linear regression models with a
train/test split and cross-validation. The second half uses simulated
nonlinear data to show why cross-validation helps choose model
complexity.

## Learning Objectives

- Create a reproducible train/test split.
- Fit and compare two regression models.
- Compute residual standard error, RMSE, and test-set $R^2$.
- Use k-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation.
- Use cross-validation to choose the degree of a polynomial model.

## Setup

The original lab used several table-formatting packages. The code below
keeps the statistical workflow lean so the resampling ideas are easier
to see.

```r
library(ISLR)
library(boot)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(571)
```

## Carseats Data

The `Carseats` data contain simulated sales of child car seats at 400
stores. The response variable is `Sales`; the remaining variables
describe pricing, advertising, shelf location, demographics, and store
context.

```r
carseats <- ISLR::Carseats
head(carseats)
summary(carseats)
```

The goal is to predict `Sales` and compare two models:

- a full model using all available predictors,
- a reduced model that excludes `Population`, `Education`, `Urban`, and
  `US`.

## Train/Test Split

A train/test split estimates how well a fitted model performs on data
that were not used to estimate its coefficients.

```r
set.seed(571)
train_id <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(carseats)),
  size = floor(0.80 * nrow(carseats))
)

train <- carseats[train_id, ]
test <- carseats[-train_id, ]
```

## Fit the Full Model

The full model uses every predictor in the data set.

```r
full_fit <- lm(Sales ~ ., data = train)
summary(full_fit)
sigma(full_fit)
```

The residual standard error estimates the typical size of a training
residual, measured in the units of `Sales`. It is useful for describing
in-sample fit, but it is not a substitute for test-set performance.

## Fit the Reduced Model

The reduced model removes four predictors and keeps the variables that
are often most directly tied to sales: competitor price, income,
advertising, price, shelf location, and age.

```r
reduced_fit <- lm(
  Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + ShelveLoc + Age,
  data = train
)

summary(reduced_fit)
sigma(reduced_fit)
```

## Test-Set Metrics

RMSE measures the typical prediction error on the test set. Test-set
$R^2$ compares the model's squared prediction error with the squared
error from always predicting the test-set mean.

```r
model_metrics <- function(fit, test_data, model_name) {
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = test_data)
  actual <- test_data$Sales

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2))
  test_r2 <- 1 - sum((actual - pred)^2) /
    sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)

  data.frame(
    model = model_name,
    residual_se = sigma(fit),
    rmse = rmse,
    test_r2 = test_r2
  )
}

bind_rows(
  model_metrics(full_fit, test, "Full model"),
  model_metrics(reduced_fit, test, "Reduced model")
)
```

When comparing models, do not rely on one number alone. A model can have
slightly better training fit but worse test performance, or similar
test performance with fewer predictors.

## Nested Model Comparison

Because the reduced model is nested inside the full model, an ANOVA
comparison can test whether the excluded variables improve the fit
enough to justify the additional complexity.

```r
anova(reduced_fit, full_fit)
```

Use the p-value to decide whether the additional predictors explain a
meaningful amount of variation after the reduced model's predictors are
already included.

## Exercise: New Split

Create a new 70/30 train/test split and repeat the comparison.

```r
set.seed(572)
train_id_70 <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(carseats)),
  size = floor(0.70 * nrow(carseats))
)

train_70 <- carseats[train_id_70, ]
test_70 <- carseats[-train_id_70, ]

full_fit_70 <- lm(Sales ~ ., data = train_70)
reduced_fit_70 <- lm(
  Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + ShelveLoc + Age,
  data = train_70
)

bind_rows(
  model_metrics(full_fit_70, test_70, "Full model, 70/30 split"),
  model_metrics(reduced_fit_70, test_70, "Reduced model, 70/30 split")
)
```

Write a short interpretation. Did the preferred model change? If it did,
explain whether the change seems meaningful or just a result of a
different random split.

## Cross-Validation with `cv.glm()`

Cross-validation reduces dependence on a single train/test split. The
`cv.glm()` function works with models fit using `glm()`. With a
Gaussian response and identity link, `glm()` gives the same fitted mean
structure as ordinary least squares.

```r
full_glm <- glm(Sales ~ ., data = carseats)
reduced_glm <- glm(
  Sales ~ CompPrice + Income + Advertising + Price + ShelveLoc + Age,
  data = carseats
)
```

### 5-Fold Cross-Validation

```r
set.seed(571)
cv5_full <- cv.glm(carseats, full_glm, K = 5)
cv5_reduced <- cv.glm(carseats, reduced_glm, K = 5)

data.frame(
  model = c("Full model", "Reduced model"),
  cv_mse = c(cv5_full$delta[1], cv5_reduced$delta[1]),
  adjusted_cv_mse = c(cv5_full$delta[2], cv5_reduced$delta[2])
)
```

### 10-Fold Cross-Validation

```r
set.seed(571)
cv10_full <- cv.glm(carseats, full_glm, K = 10)
cv10_reduced <- cv.glm(carseats, reduced_glm, K = 10)

data.frame(
  model = c("Full model", "Reduced model"),
  cv_mse = c(cv10_full$delta[1], cv10_reduced$delta[1]),
  adjusted_cv_mse = c(cv10_full$delta[2], cv10_reduced$delta[2])
)
```

### Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation

When `K` is omitted, `cv.glm()` uses leave-one-out cross-validation.

```r
loocv_full <- cv.glm(carseats, full_glm)
loocv_reduced <- cv.glm(carseats, reduced_glm)

data.frame(
  model = c("Full model", "Reduced model"),
  loocv_mse = c(loocv_full$delta[1], loocv_reduced$delta[1]),
  adjusted_loocv_mse = c(loocv_full$delta[2], loocv_reduced$delta[2])
)
```

Lower cross-validation error indicates better estimated
out-of-sample performance. If the two values are very close, prefer the
model that is easier to explain unless there is a strong reason to keep
the larger model.

## Simulated Nonlinear Data

The second part of the lab uses data generated from a nonlinear
relationship. This makes it possible to see why a straight line can be
too simple and a very high-degree polynomial can be too flexible.

```r
set.seed(571)
sim_data <- data.frame(x = runif(100, min = -10, max = 10))
sim_data$y <- sin(sim_data$x) + 0.1 * sim_data$x^2 + rnorm(100)

ggplot(sim_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#336699") +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y")
```

## Linear Model for the Simulated Data

```r
linear_sim <- glm(y ~ x, data = sim_data)

set.seed(571)
linear_cv <- cv.glm(sim_data, linear_sim, K = 10)
linear_cv$delta
```

The first value in `delta` is the estimated cross-validation error. The
second is an adjusted version intended to reduce bias in the estimate.

## Polynomial Models

A polynomial model adds powers of `x` to allow curvature. The
`poly()` function constructs a numerically stable polynomial basis.

```r
quadratic_sim <- glm(y ~ poly(x, 2), data = sim_data)

set.seed(571)
quadratic_cv <- cv.glm(sim_data, quadratic_sim, K = 10)
quadratic_cv$delta
```

Now compare polynomial degrees from 1 through 15.

```r
set.seed(571)
degree_errors <- data.frame(
  degree = 1:15,
  cv_mse = NA_real_
)

for (degree in degree_errors$degree) {
  fit <- glm(y ~ poly(x, degree), data = sim_data)
  degree_errors$cv_mse[degree] <- cv.glm(
    sim_data,
    fit,
    K = 10
  )$delta[1]
}

degree_errors
```

```r
ggplot(degree_errors, aes(x = degree, y = cv_mse)) +
  geom_line(color = "#336699") +
  geom_point(color = "#336699") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:15) +
  labs(
    x = "Polynomial degree",
    y = "10-fold CV mean squared error"
  )
```

## Interpretation Questions

1. Which polynomial degree has the lowest cross-validation error?
2. Does the lowest-error model also look like the best explanatory
   model?
3. What happens to cross-validation error when the polynomial degree is
   very high?
4. How would your answer change if interpretability mattered more than
   predictive accuracy?
